Hirsute simply means very hairy — but it's not just any kind of hairy. It specifically describes something or someone covered in a noticeably large amount of hair, or hair that is thick, coarse, and rough to the touch. Think of it as the more precise, formal upgrade of the word "hairy."
What Makes It Different From Just "Hairy"

If you call someone "hairy," you're stating a plain fact. If you call them "hirsute," you're saying the same thing, but with more weight — implying that the hair is abundant and conspicuous enough to be the first thing you notice. It suggests a kind of ruggedness or shagginess, not just the presence of hair.

Hirsute is most commonly used to describe:

  • People — A man with a thick, bushy beard and dense chest hair could be described as hirsute. A woman with noticeably heavy body hair might also be described this way.
  • Animals — A shaggy, heavily furred creature like a bear or a musk ox could be called hirsute.
  • Plants (less commonly) — In biology and botany, it describes plant surfaces covered in stiff, coarse hairs or bristles, like certain leaves or stems.
The Register: When and Where Is This Word Used?

Hirsute is a formal and literary word. You will rarely hear it in everyday conversation. It tends to appear in:

  • Written prose — novels, essays, journalism, or descriptive writing where the author wants a sophisticated, vivid word.
  • Humorous writing — sometimes used with a slightly playful or tongue-in-cheek tone, poking gentle fun at someone's hairiness in a clever way rather than a rude one.
  • Scientific or biological writing — particularly in botany and zoology.
Connotation: Is It Positive, Negative, or Neutral?

Hirsute is largely neutral, but it leans ever so slightly toward describing something that looks rough, wild, or untamed because of the excess hair. It is not an insult on its own, but the context around it shapes the tone. A writer describing a rugged mountain man as hirsute might be conveying admiration, humor, or simple observation — it depends entirely on how the word is framed.

• "The hirsute actor was instantly recognizable on screen, his thick beard and bushy eyebrows giving him an unmistakable look."
  • "She scratched the hirsute dog behind its ears, her fingers disappearing into its thick, coarse fur."
  • "He was a broad, hirsute man — the kind you'd expect to find splitting logs in the forest, not arranging flowers."
  • "The botanist noted that the plant's hirsute leaves were an adaptation to cold mountain climates."
A Simple Way to Remember It

Picture the most noticeably, dramatically hairy person or animal you can imagine — the kind where the hair itself is a defining feature of their appearance. That image is hirsute. It's not subtle hairiness. It's the kind that stands out.
